summary: Direct, parallel, pilot and phased implementation — how each works, when to use it, and a comparison of their advantages and disadvantages.

items.title: Direct changeover
items.content: The old system is switched off and the new one is used **immediately**.

items.title: Parallel running
items.content: Old and new systems **run together**; results are compared until the new system is trusted.

items.title: Pilot implementation
items.content: The full new system is used **in one part** of the organisation first (one branch, one class, one department).

items.title: Phased implementation
items.content: The new system replaces the old one **module by module** across the organisation.

rows: Risk if the new system fails
Easy — compare outputs of both systems

blocks.title: Choosing a method from the situation
rows: Ship-arrival tracking at a seaport — the system must never fail
A school replaces a paper log for hobby clubs, trying it with some clubs first
A café starts taking orders on tablets instead of at the counter
A chain of supermarkets introduces a new stock-control system in one shop
A university introduces a new system: admissions this year, timetables next term, finance later
The old system has completely broken down

blocks.content: Justify the choice with a reason linked to **risk**, **cost** or **structure**: "Parallel, **because** errors in tracking ships could be dangerous, and the old system acts as a **backup** while the new one is checked."
